area: The not-found decision: when search should return nothing. Today the rule is to return nothing when the best dense cosine is below 0.50.
idea:
Recommendation: NO CHANGE. Keep the single dense floor at min_score 0.50.

I tested 22 refusal rules on top of today's floor, plus a no-floor reference. They fall into seven families: a different floor; the gap between the best and 10th dense section; the gap between the best and 10th scheme; whether the word and letter channels agree with the dense winner; how far the best score stands above the corpus-average cosine, in raw points and in standard deviations (z); and how spread out the top 5 sections are. To check that the offline replay was right, I ran three rules end to end through the shared harness: today's rule, floor 0.54, and the agreement gate at 0.56. The other 19 were evaluated offline from the same scores.

Where things stand at 54 schemes: off-topic questions are 6/6 refused. Three not-found questions still get evidence, and they are all English questions that name a state scheme the corpus does not contain (KALIA, Rythu Bharosa, Kanya Sumangala). Their best dense scores are 0.535, 0.586 and 0.619. The lowest-scoring answerable question whose answer does reach the prompt scores 0.567, at both sizes. Nine answerable questions at 54 score between 0.55 and 0.60, and almost all of them are Hindi or Hinglish. The scores overlap, so no single number can separate the two groups.

Why it is hard: these "absent scheme" questions are on topic (they ask about eligibility for a farmer or girl-child scheme). The dense model therefore matches them to the "eligibility rules" section of similar schemes. The usual warning signs for "this doesn't fit" (a small gap to the runners-up, the word channels disagreeing, top sections spread over many schemes) also fire for Hindi and Hinglish answerable questions. Those questions get lower, flatter dense scores because the corpus is in English, and the word channels miss them too.

Only two rules cost nothing on dev at either size, and they make the same decisions on dev: floor 0.54, and refusing when the best score is below 0.56 and neither word channel supports the winner. Both gain exactly 1 not-found question at 54 (KALIA in English, at 0.535). They gain nothing at scale and change no in-prompt result.

I do not recommend even floor 0.54:
(1) It puts the threshold just above one question. That is the overfitting pattern the task warns against, and the gain is 1 of 12.
(2) Smoothing the answerable score distribution predicts about 0.7 to 1.0 answerable questions per 304 landing in [0.50, 0.54) on unseen questions. Dev has none there, but the tail is thin and made of Hindi and Hinglish situation questions. The expected loss roughly equals the expected gain.
(3) The two mistakes are not equally bad. Wrongly refusing a real question is a hard failure. An on-topic question about an absent scheme still reaches an answer model that is told to say when the information is missing, and the sections it sees are visibly about a different named scheme.
(4) eval_config.yaml already records that 0.54 is the strictest value that loses nothing on dev, and that 0.50 was kept on purpose as a safety margin. These results give no reason to give up that margin.

Lowering the floor gains nothing either. The one answerable dev question it refuses at 54 (a Hinglish situation question at 0.480) does not get its answer into the prompt even with no floor at all.

At scale: the 6 "absent" questions really do find same-named background schemes (KALIA, Kanya Sumangala, Rythu Bima), so their abstention cannot be judged there. Off-topic is 5/6. The one miss, "aaj mausam kaisa hai?", scores 0.562, only 0.005 below the lowest answerable question at scale (0.567). No floor can safely catch it.
general_argument:
Any rule that would hold for an arbitrary corpus of scheme documents in a mix of languages has to work from score-shape signals: the absolute score, the gaps to runners-up, how far the winner stands above the corpus, whether the channels agree, and how spread out the top results are. I measured all of these. None separates "asks about a scheme that is not here" from "answerable question in a different language than the documents". Cross-language questions push dense scores down and flatten them, and the word channels miss them, so every family above refuses them first.

The remaining failures are an entity problem, not a score problem: the question names a specific scheme and the corpus has no scheme by that name. A general fix would compare the scheme names mentioned in the question against the corpus titles and aliases. That needs name detection that works across languages, which I did not try because it is outside score-based gating and risks hand-built rules. The answer model, which sees the retrieved section titles, is the natural second gate for this case.

A change worth making should be backed by more than one dev question and should help at both sizes. Floor 0.54 is backed by exactly one question and does nothing at scale, so no change is the conservative, general choice.
implementation:

class AgreementGateRetriever(Retriever):
    def __init__(self, pack, agree_below=0.56, lexical_top=5, **kw):
        super().__init__(pack, **kw)
        self.agree_below, self.lexical_top = agree_below, lexical_top
    def _top_schemes(self, scores, n):
        out = []
        for i in self._top(scores, self.depth):
            key = self.documents[i].scheme_key
            if key not in out:
                out.append(key)
                if len(out) == n: break
        return out
    def _rank(self, query, top_k):
        sims, order = super()._rank(query, top_k)          # keeps the 0.50 floor
        if sims is None or len(order) == 0 or sims.max() >= self.agree_below:
            return sims, order
        best = self.documents[int(np.argmax(sims))].scheme_key
        lexical = self._expand(query) if self._glossary else query
        for scores in (self._bm25.scores(lexical), self._char_scores(lexical)):
            if best in self._top_schemes(scores, self.lexical_top):
                return sims, order
        return sims, np.empty(0, dtype=int)                 # weak dense winner with no word support: refuse

area: How the three search channels (BM25 words, letter runs, dense meaning) are merged into one ranking: score-aware fusion that respects how far ahead the dense match is.
idea: Keep the current weighted rank fusion, but add one rule: word and letter matches may only reorder sections whose meaning similarity is close to the best one, within a margin m=0.05 in cosine units. Sections that meaning search puts clearly further behind can no longer be lifted above them. In practice, the sections within 0.05 of the best dense cosine go first, in their normal fused order, and every other section follows, also in fused order. With no margin set, the ranking is exactly today's. The abstention check (best dense cosine below 0.50, so nothing is retrieved) runs before fusion and is unchanged, so abstention cannot change. The runner-up family was a convex score combination: dense cosine + 0.10 x (word and letter scores, each divided by its best score for that question).
general_argument: Rank fusion turns each channel's scores into ranks, so a 0.29 cosine lead and a 0.001 lead look the same. The word channel (BM25) and the letter channel (char n-grams) both measure word overlap, so they tend to agree with each other. Together they can outvote the meaning channel even when meaning has a decisive lead. This hurts most when the question's language or script differs from the documents': the overlap a Hindi question has with English text (a shared word like yojana in aliases, numbers, acronyms) is mostly accidental, while a multilingual embedder still measures meaning reliably. The gate says that word matches settle near-ties in meaning but never override a clear meaning preference. That rule uses no scheme ids, names, wording, language detection or glossary changes, and it applies to any document corpus in any language mix. The margin is in the embedder's own cosine units, the same footing as the existing min_score threshold, so it is re-checked whenever the embedder or query instruction changes. Evidence that it is general and not fitted to these questions: (1) at 54 schemes all 6 fixes are the known pattern, where the right scheme led on meaning by 0.10-0.29 and was pushed out by weak word matches (e.g. jssk 0.625 vs nfsa_pmgkay 0.521, nikshay_poshan 0.757 vs igndps 0.465). (2) Margins 0.05 and 0.10 give identical results at 54 (+6, 0 broken). (3) The gate is a strict restriction of today's ranking: it only ever moves toward meaning order when meaning's lead is larger than the margin, so what it can change is limited and easy to predict. (4) It helps at both corpus sizes, and the scale corpus behaves like a much larger, noisier corpus.
implementation:
Algorithm (fusion branch of Retriever._rank): meaning = dense cosines. If meaning.max() < min_score, return nothing (unchanged). fused = weighted RRF over the bm25, char and dense top-`depth` lists (unchanged). If fusion_dense_margin is set: near = (meaning >= meaning.max() - margin) & (fused > 0); fused[near] += fused.max(). Then take the top k as today. The offset fused.max() guarantees every near section scores above every other section while keeping RRF order inside each group. For k <= depth this is identical to a hard two-group sort, because the dense top-`depth` list always contains the best near sections.

area: Ranking schemes rather than sections, and assembling the 3-section evidence (retrieve_evidence), tested on top of the current fusion ranking and on top of plain dense ranking
idea: Choose the scheme first, then fill the 3 prompt slots. The section-level ranking stays exactly as it is today. (1) Each scheme gets a score: its best section's fused (rank-fusion) score plus 0.5 times its second-best section's score. (2) Meaning lead: if the scheme with the highest meaning similarity (cosine, its best section) is at least 0.10 above the fusion leader's, it becomes the leader. (3) Admission: another scheme may take slots only if its best meaning similarity is within 0.03 of the leader's, or above it, with at most one scheme per slot, taken in scheme-score order. Otherwise those slots go to the leader's next-best sections. (4) Fill: the leader's rules first, then the admitted schemes' sections best-first by fused score, each section bringing its scheme's rules before it (today's rule). If the admitted schemes run out of sections, the walk continues over the rest in rank order, so the prompt is never emptier than today. The min_score abstain gate, top_k=3, and retrieve() are unchanged. With the setting absent, the evidence is identical to today's at both sizes (checked on all 316 dev questions).
general_argument:
Every part uses only document structure that any scheme corpus has (a scheme_id grouping sections and a rules label) and the calibrated cosine scale the pipeline already relies on for min_score. Nothing depends on scheme names, question wording, language or a glossary.
(a) A document that is really about the question usually matches in several of its sections (overview, benefits, rules). A single stray section of another document that shares a few words or an alias matches in one. Scoring a document by its best section plus a fraction of its second-best is the standard MaxP plus a small multi-passage bonus from passage-level IR. Only 0.5 is used, not a sum, because a sum would favour schemes with many sections; the scale corpus has schemes with up to 13.
(b) Reciprocal rank fusion throws away score magnitudes, so two weak word matches can outrank a much closer meaning match. When the meaning channel says one scheme is clearly closer (by 0.10 cosine, on the same scale where 0.50 already decides "answer or abstain"), trusting it is a confidence-aware override that applies in any language.
(c) Slots are scarce (3), and every scheme brings its rules. Giving a slot to a scheme that is clearly less similar in meaning costs the leader a section that more often holds the answer. Admitting only near-ties keeps sibling schemes (two pensions, two housing schemes) side by side, which is when the answer model needs to see both.
Robustness, not tuned for any of these settings: on top of four different fusion settings the recommended variant gained +6 to +12 at 54 and +3 to +12 at scale, breaking at most 1. On plain dense ranking it is neutral at 54 and +6/-0 at scale. Nearby values give the same or nearly the same result: admit_gap 0.03, 0.06 and 0.10 all give 288/304 at 54 with 0 broken, and second_weight 1.0 gives 287 and 265.

area: Representation: what text each retrieval channel sees. This covers (a) contextual section text for the dense index, (b) the lexical query view (vocabulary restriction, dropping Devanagari, coverage weighting, and a new idea: romanising Indian-script words), and (c) the wording of the dense query instruction.
idea:
The letter-run channel (character 3-5-gram TF-IDF) also gets a Latin spelling of every Indian-script word in the question. "निक्षय पोषण योजना ..." is searched as itself plus "nikshay poshan yojna ...", and "जननी शिशु सुरक्षा कार्यक्रम" also as "janani shishu suraksha karyakram". The romaniser is rule-based and has no parameters, about 100 lines with no new dependency. One table covers all nine Brahmic Unicode blocks, because they share the ISCII layout. It writes the informal spelling people type (sh/ch/chh, long vowels as short, फ as f) and applies Hindi schwa deletion (final, plus a conservative medial rule). Nothing else changes. BM25 and the dense query see exactly what they see today. The abstain gate is dense-only, so abstention cannot change. Questions with no Indian-script words (English and romanised-Hindi questions) get identical results by construction.

Why it helps: in the dev failures, Hindi questions name schemes that the documents spell only in Latin letters (Ni-kshay Poshan, Janani Shishu Suraksha), or whose Devanagari aliases share words with a twin scheme (PM Kisan and PM Kisan Maan-dhan). The lexical channels could only see generic in-vocabulary words such as योजना, के, लिए and the glossary's "scheme yojana". So their votes went to whichever sections matched those words (failure pattern 1). With a romanised copy, the spelling-tolerant channel can match the scheme name itself.
general_argument:
Indian scheme corpora, like most government corpora in multilingual countries, are mainly written in English and spell local names and terms in Latin letters (Yojana, Kisan, Poshan, Awas, Bima). Users often type the same words in their own script. Matching across scripts is a known problem in code-mixed and transliterated search, for example the FIRE mixed-script IR tasks. Transliterating the query is the standard remedy.

The mechanism uses only Unicode structure: no scheme ids, names, question wording or glossary entries. It works for any language mix:
- Latin-only questions: a no-op.
- A corpus written in Devanagari: the original words stay in the query, so nothing is lost.
- Bengali, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Oriya, Kannada and other Brahmic scripts: the same offset table applies.

It goes only to the letter-run channel because that channel is built to tolerate approximate spellings. A rule-based romanisation is approximate ("rashtriy" vs "rashtriya", "yojna" vs "yojana", "penshan" vs "pension"). Exact-word BM25 gains little from it and can be hit by romanised function words.

Question-free check, which uses corpus aliases only and never the evaluation questions (alias_check.py): each scheme's Devanagari alias was romanised and searched in the corpus's Latin-script text only.
- 54 schemes: the right scheme comes first in 37/47 cases and in the top 5 in 44/47.
- About 4,650 schemes: first in 23/47, top 5 in 39/47.
- Searching with the raw Devanagari: 0/47.

Honesty notes:
- The romaniser has no tunable parameters and was frozen before any dev measurement. I did choose its conventions (फ→f, keep the final a after a conjunct ending in y/r/v/l, medial schwa deletion only from the third letter) by looking at its output on a word list that included some scheme words from failing questions. These are standard romanisation conventions, with no per-word exceptions.
- Only three "where to feed it" variants were tried (char only, char+BM25, char+BM25 with the glossary applied to the romanised words), and all are reported. The simplest one, char only, was the only one with zero breaks at both sizes.

Algorithm of romanise_word:
- Map each code point by its offset within its block (offset = ord(ch) - block_start, blocks 0x0900, 0x0980, ..., 0x0D00) through the CONSONANTS, VOWELS and SIGNS tables. Consonants carry an inherent "a".
- Virama removes it; a vowel sign replaces it; a nukta changes the consonant (ज़->z, ड़->r, फ़->f).
- Anusvara/candrabindu -> "n" ("m" before p/b/m); visarga -> "h"; native digits -> 0-9.
- Schwa deletion: drop the final consonant's "a", unless the word ends in a conjunct whose last letter is y/r/v/l. Drop a medial "a" in a V C _ C V context (Ohala), from the third letter on.

(2) The scale gain shrinks as the margin grows: +5/-1 at 0.04, +4/-1 at 0.05, +2/-1 at 0.06 (my probe), 0/0 at 0.10. The single break appears at every margin from 0.04 to 0.06.

preregistered_keep_rule:
Written before any official round. Candidate values are frozen as proposed: romanise_char has no parameters; fusion_dense_margin is 0.05; scheme_first is {second_weight 0.5, admit_gap 0.03, lead_gap 0.10}. Nothing is retuned after seeing a round's numbers. A failed round is undone whole and is not retried with new values in this cycle.

How a round is run: one change per round, measured against the LAST KEPT state (not the original baseline). Use the shared harness on DEV only, at both 54 schemes and scale, with the same embedder, query instruction, min_score 0.50 and top_k 3.

KEEP only if every item in A holds at BOTH sizes, and then every item in B holds. Otherwise UNDO.

A. Retrieval guards (stricter than the search rule in scripts/compare_runs.py, which tolerates a 1-question slice loss):
A1. Gain: net in-prompt (fixed minus broken) is at least +1 at each size.
A2. Breaks: at most 1 broken question per size. Each break gets a written explanation of the mechanism, and no per-question fix is allowed.
A3. Slices, zero tolerance: no language slice (en, hi, hi_latn) and no type slice (fact, eligibility, situation, typo) has a lower in-prompt count than the kept state, at either size.
A4. Not-found: the number of not-found questions refused does not go down, and the number of answerable questions refused does not go up, at either size.
A5. The number of answerable questions whose gold scheme reaches the prompt does not go down at either size.
A6. The harness's scheme-level 95% CI lower bound is at least 0 at each size.
A7. Budget robustness: in-prompt at top_k 2 and at top_k 5 is not lower than the kept state at either size. This guards against fitting to exactly 3 slots.
A8. Out-of-sample sanity: on the 206 fine-tuning questions that are not in dev (data/training/india_schemes/sft_train.jsonl and sft_dev.jsonl), scored by whether the asked scheme reaches the prompt, there is no new miss and no new refusal at either size.
A9. Cost: retrieval-only time is at most 2x the kept state and at most 10 ms per question at scale. The scale corpus is not re-embedded.

B. End-to-end answer check (required before a KEEP is final):
Run scripts/evaluate_pipeline.py --split dev --runs fusion for the kept state and for the candidate, at 54 and at scale (--corpus), with the deployed answer model (Qwen3.5-0.8B, greedy, seed 42). Then run scripts/compare_runs.py <before> <after> --run fusion at each size.
B1. Determinism: every question whose evidence did not change must get an identical answer. If not, the run is invalid and is repeated.
B2. The dev answer pass count and the weighted answer score (coverage 0.35, follow-up 0.25, groundedness 0.25, actionability 0.15) are not lower at either size. No language or type slice loses a passing answer net.
B3. Safety: zero new gate violations (forbidden_claim, false_confirmation / unsafe 'yes') at either size.
B4. No not-found question that was previously declined is now answered.
B5. The compare_runs.py answer verdict is not UNDO. NO CLEAR DIFFERENCE is acceptable only if B1 to B4 all hold.

C. Logging: record every round, including undone ones, with all numbers at both sizes, the fixed and broken question ids, the mechanism, and the decision. The test split is run once after the last round, on the final kept configuration against the original baseline, reported whatever it shows, and never used to choose or undo.
